cards.title: Delegate problems back: ask for the F-I-X after the A-W-K
cards.summary: For routine store problems, ask the accountable owner to propose options while keeping urgent escalation open.
cards.use_when: A team member (merchandiser, buyer, store manager, fulfillment lead) escalates a problem to you — a stockout, a listing error, a supplier delay — and waits for you to solve it.
steps: For a routine merchandising, replenishment or creative issue, ask what solutions the owner sees and what help they need.
Have the owner compare options and recommend a next step within their authority.
Add context and coaching without automatically taking over the work.
For a live checkout failure, customer harm or other urgent incident, accept the escalation immediately even when no solution is known.
Agree who owns the fix, the deadline and when to escalate again.
caveats: This is a management habit, not a rule about withholding help. The source still has managers engage and support — the point is who owns the fix.
For genuinely novel or high-risk decisions (a platform migration, a major supplier contract), insisting on a fix before any guidance can waste time; supply context first.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Let natural consequences teach instead of rescuing your team
cards.summary: Use bounded, recoverable ecommerce assignments for learning instead of automatically taking over every difficult task.
cards.use_when: An owner or manager is tempted to jump in and rescue a campaign, listing, launch, or supplier negotiation that a team member is handling poorly.
steps: Pick smaller waves. The source's guidance is explicit that you do not need to let a major project fail — choose teaching moments whose consequences are instructive but not catastrophic (a small test campaign, one channel, a minor vendor).
Let it happen: don't fix the assignment so it doesn't fail, don't take over a meeting because someone is handling it badly, let the person experience a degree of failure.
Talk about it afterward: be available immediately after the failed meeting or lost deal to help them get up and analyze what happened. Ask good questions and avoid 'I told you so.'
Focus on next time: help them find a way to succeed on the next comparable situation — e.g. ask how they'll handle a similar negotiation with another supplier already in the pipeline.
Also let good decisions run: step out of the way, give credit, and let people reap the full benefits of their wins, not just the consequences of their losses.

The source contrasts this with a manager who reworks a subordinate's key presentation at the last minute or intervenes the moment an internal customer is unhappy — those interventions signal the person isn't capable and often reduce their effort next time.
caveats: Agree limits before the assignment; intervene if customer harm, uncontrolled spend or a critical operational failure is developing.
This is the source's coaching principle, not proof that deliberate failure produces faster learning in every team.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Define ownership with an explicit vote split and a stretched role
cards.summary: Hand over real accountability for an end result, not piecemeal tasks, and make the ownership share concrete with a number.
cards.use_when: You are assigning a team member to own a recurring ecommerce outcome — a category P&L, a channel, a subscription program — and want them to run with it.
steps: Name the lead explicitly. Say that they, not you, are in charge and accountable for the end goal; explain how you will stay engaged and support them, but that they remain in charge.
Make it concrete with a number: the source suggests telling them they have 51 percent of the vote and you have only 49 percent, or being bolder with a 75/25 split.
Give ownership of the current scope of their role and then take it up one level — look for ways to up-level responsibility and hand someone a job they aren't fully qualified for.
Avoid delegating piecemeal tasks but not real responsibility. The source's Micromanager gives people just a piece of the puzzle and then wonders why they can't assemble it without them.
Example: instead of asking a merchandiser to update prices on ten SKUs, give them ownership of the category's margin and let them decide the pricing moves; you review outcomes, not keystrokes.
caveats: The 51/49 and 75/25 splits are the source's illustrative devices, not measured thresholds.
Stretching someone into a role they aren't qualified for requires you to actually stay available as backup, or the stretch becomes abandonment.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Hand back the pen: offer help with a built-in exit
cards.summary: When you jump in to help someone who is stuck, plan the moment you symbolically return control so they stay accountable for finishing.
cards.use_when: A team member asks for your opinion on a campaign, launch plan, or supplier decision and you can feel yourself about to take over.
steps: Before entering the conversation, visualize the point where you will give the pen back — imagine adding a few ideas at the whiteboard and then physically handing the marker over.

Offer your help and then explicitly return the lead using the source's phrases: 'I'm happy to help think this through, but I'm still looking to you to lead this going forward'; 'You are still in the lead on this'; 'I'm here to back you up'; 'What do you need from me as you lead this?'
The source notes some leaders' urge to take over is so strong they sit on their hands, afraid to speak at all — the goal is calibrated input plus an explicit exit, not silence.
After the conversation, confirm the owner still has the next action, not you.
Applies to a one-on-one, a hallway conversation, or a launch review; the venue doesn't matter, the handoff does.
caveats: Without the explicit verbal handoff, your ideas will be read as instructions and you'll be back in the driver's seat.
This is the source's advice for capable people who are stuck, not a substitute for stepping in when someone is genuinely out of their depth on a critical decision.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Make the scoreboard visible so people manage themselves
cards.summary: Post clear, per-person performance metrics publicly and the team drives its own improvement without the manager pushing.
cards.use_when: You want a team (supply chain, CS, paid media, merchandising) to raise performance without a manager constantly chasing them.
steps: Follow the source's coaching example — Jubin Dana, a lawyer and soccer coach, keeps and posts player stats. Do the same for each role: track a small set of performance numbers that are comparable across the team.

Examples by function: for a paid media buyer, track spend, ROAS, and creative win rate; for a CS team, first-response time and resolution rate; for replenishment, stockout days and forecast accuracy; for merchandising, attach rate and sell-through.
Post all the stats where the whole team can see them, per person, so each person can tell where they rank and where they need to improve.
Then stop yelling. The source's point is that once players have the information they push themselves to higher levels; the coach's urging becomes redundant.
Visible measures of success 'liberate and focus intelligence and energy' — the scoreboard is the mechanism that lets you reduce direct supervision without losing performance.
To hold people accountable, pair the scoreboard with defined ownership: the owner of a metric is named, and the metric is what they answer for.
caveats: Publicly posting individual stats can demotivate in some cultures; the source treats visibility as universally energizing, which is an assumption, not a tested finding for every team.
Metrics must be ones the person actually controls, or the scoreboard becomes blame rather than information.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Avoid the bungee-boss pattern: jumping in and out destroys ownership
cards.summary: Leaders who only engage when a problem has executive visibility create dependency and disengagement on the rest of the work.
cards.use_when: You are triaging your own attention across ecommerce workstreams and catch yourself only engaging with the high-visibility projects.
steps: Recognize the pattern the source calls the Micromanager who jumps in and out: they hand over work but take it back the moment problems arise, appearing 'all over it' when a senior executive is watching and 'completely absent' otherwise.

Check your own week: which projects get your attention only because the CEO or board will see them? The source's example — a CMO who took over anything with CEO visibility and disappeared on work that formed the backbone of the business — is the archetype.
Fix it structurally: give owners a defined scope and a visible scoreboard (see separate card) instead of relying on your own attention as the monitoring mechanism.
Have a defined engagement protocol instead of random strikes: state up front how and when you will be involved, so the owner knows they carry the work between checkpoints.
The source names the failure modes explicitly: dependency, disengagement, and 'disruptive chaos' when the leader strikes at random.
caveats: Multipliers do get involved in operational details — the source's own unexpected finding — but they keep ownership with other people. Disengagement is not the fix; the fix is predictable, ownership-preserving involvement.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Run staff reviews as debates on the jugular issues, not report-outs
cards.summary: Replace functional status meetings with pre-circulated strategic questions the team debates with data and an owner assigned to each outcome.
cards.use_when: You run a recurring ecommerce leadership meeting that has become a series of functional status updates with no decisions.
steps: Take the source's Bill Campbell coaching example: he told a CEO, 'You are not getting anything out of these staff meetings. You need to engage your people on your biggest issues.'

Before the meeting, have the CEO prepare five topics crucial to the company and email the list to the team in advance, asking each person to think through the issues and arrive with data and opinions.
Open the meeting by asking the team to take off their functional hat and put their company hat on — e.g. on an ecommerce team, the question might be: should we fulfill in-house or hand it to a 3PL?
Let executives argue both sides; the CEO listens carefully, makes the decision, and then outlines implications and actions.
Have an owner step up immediately to take the decision forward ('I've got it. I'll take it from here.'), then move to the next topic and the next debate.
This converts meetings from information transfer into decision-making with distributed ownership.
caveats: This is the source's account of Campbell's coaching work with a specific client, not a measured benchmark.
Advance preparation is the load-bearing step; without pre-circulated questions and data, the debate degrades back into a report-out.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Adopt the assumption first and let behavior follow
cards.summary: Changing your underlying belief about people's capability knocks out whole sets of micromanaging behaviors, like hitting the head pin in bowling.
cards.use_when: You are trying to change your own or a manager's behavior on an ecommerce team but individual techniques aren't sticking.
steps: Work from the source's bowling analogy: the assumptions are the head pin — knock them down and the behaviors behind them fall with them.

Try on the Multiplier assumptions as a set: 'If I can find someone's genius, I can put them to work' (Talent Magnet); 'People's best thinking must be given, not taken' (Liberator); 'People get smarter by being challenged' (Challenger); 'With enough minds, we can figure it out' (Debate Maker); 'People are smart and will figure things out' (Investor).

Test it in a live decision. The source's example: you assign a marketer to a cross-divisional task force. Under the Diminisher assumption ('people will never figure it out without me'), she becomes your eyes and ears, avoids controversy, and your division's interests get decided without you. Under the Multiplier assumption, you tell her she's chosen for her market understanding, she represents the whole division, she is fully responsible for implementing the outcomes, and you're available as a sounding board.
Note the source is candid that the chart supplied in the book appears to swap the Investo assumptions; the intended Multiplier belief is that people are smart and will figure it out.
Once assumptions shift, the source reports leaders stop feeling like a bottleneck and start asking 'How can I improve the situation without putting myself at the center?'
caveats: The task-force scenario is the source's illustrative example showing divergent outcomes, not a documented ecommerce result.
Assumptions are being asked to do a lot of work here; if the surrounding incentive system punishes initiative, beliefs alone won't change outcomes.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Work the extremes: neutralize a weakness, top off a strength
cards.summary: Aspiring multipliers should develop only at the two extremes — fix a show-stopper weakness and turn one strength into a towering one — and ignore the middle.
cards.use_when: You are planning your own or a manager's development after a performance review or 360, and feel overwhelmed by the full list of feedback.
steps: Use the source's evidence base: Zenger and Folkman's study of 360 data for 8,000 leaders found leaders with no distinguishing strength rated at the 34th percentile of effectiveness; one strength (with no sharp weakness) jumped them to the 64th; two, three and four strengths reached the 72nd, 81st and 89th percentiles.

Apply the source's own observation about multipliers: most were strong in just three of five disciplines, and rarely in the Diminisher range on any. Strength in three disciplines appears to be the threshold; you don't need all five.
Neutralize a weakness. Don't try to turn your biggest weakness into a strength. Aim only to move it into the middle, acceptable zone — you just can't be bad.
Top off a strength. Identify your strongest area and build a deep repertoire there — become world-class in one discipline rather than thoroughly average across all.

Use the source's Spencer Kaplan example as a template: his 360 showed a strength (trusted advisor, ego-free, cross-functional) and a vulnerability (capability gap between him and his team). He addressed the vulnerability first with Investor practices — real ownership, expanded roles, expecting complete work — then topped off the strength by extending into Debate Maker practices.
Deliberately disregard most other feedback so your development energy concentrates on the two extremes.
caveats: The Zenger-Folkman percentile figures come from a 2002 360-degree study of 8,000 leaders reported in The Extraordinary Leader; transplanting percentiles to a specific ecommerce team is not warranted.
The 'strength in three of five disciplines' threshold is the author's observation from studying multipliers, not a measured cutoff.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Run a 30-day single-practice challenge to build a new habit
cards.summary: Pick one practice in one discipline and work it deliberately for thirty days, journaling what works, rather than attempting a wholesale leadership overhaul.
cards.use_when: You or a manager have resolved to lead differently but feel overwhelmed and need a sustainable first step.
steps: Pick one practice within one discipline — not the whole framework. The source explicitly warns that trying to apply all five disciplines all the time will exhaust effort with little progress and end in giving up.
Commit to thirty days. The source cites research that approximately thirty days of concentrated effort forms a new habit.
Record your experiences in a journal, learning from what works and what doesn't — the source frames this as behaving like a researcher.

Apply it to concrete ecommerce management: if you choose the Investor practice 'ask for the F-I-X,' spend the month requiring proposed fixes before you engage with escalated problems; if you choose visible scoreboards, spend the month building and posting one team's metrics.
Let successful small experiments fuel the next, slightly bigger one; the source's own accelerator list includes working the extremes, starting with the assumptions, and this 30-day challenge.
caveats: The thirty-day figure is cited from general habit research, not a leadership-development study.
The source's multi-rater assessment referenced at multipliersbook.com is an external tool; verify it is still available before pointing a team to it.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Build leaders so you can step away without losing performance
cards.summary: Investing in successors is what earns a leader the right to leave without the organization falling apart — the opposite of the micromanager, whose exit crumbles the operation.
cards.use_when: You are planning a transition out of an operating role, preparing a deputy, or deciding whether to keep control of key ecommerce decisions.
steps: Follow the source's Infosys example: Narayana Murthy deliberately spent years investing in his cofounders so they could operate independently, then stepped down as CEO on his sixtieth birthday with no crisis and no power play, staying on as nonexecutive chairman and chief mentor.
Treat 'ensuring successive generations of leaders' as the primary role, in Murthy's words, rather than holding the spotlight.
Check yourself against the source's description of the micromanager's exit: when diminishers leave, things fall apart because they held the operation together with micromanagement and sweat equity.

Build independence deliberately: define ownership, invest resources, hold people accountable, and keep rolling ownership back to others. The source calls this being an Investor; when the organization is truly autonomous, the leader has earned the right to step away.
The source frames the payoff as repeatable: leaders who invest this way become Serial Multipliers, able to apply the same approach in a new venture or a new portfolio company.
caveats: The Murthy and Infosys narrative is a case example, not evidence that any founder can step away on a fixed timetable.

The source's 2X-capability claim and its extrapolation to '500 extra people' across ten roles is the author's arithmetic built on the average multiplier effect, not a measured calculation — treat it as rhetorical.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Manage a capability gap between a strong performer and their team
cards.summary: When one person outpaces their team, invest in the team first — otherwise the organization cannot expand that person's scope.
cards.use_when: A star operator (a buyer, growth marketer, or ops lead) wants a bigger role but their team isn't growing behind them.
steps: Read the signal in the source's Spencer Kaplan case: the organization viewed him as a rock star, but peers and bosses were concerned the capability gap between him and his team was too large; stakeholders said they could not expand his role unless his team members grew their abilities as fast as he did.

Address the gap before the promotion. The source's plan put investing in his immediate team first, using Investor practices: give real ownership to the team, expand their roles, and expect complete work.
After handing over greater ownership, step back and coach rather than correcting — allow natural consequences to develop them.
Then extend the person's own scope into an adjacent strength (for Spencer, from trusted advisor to debate leader) once the team gap is closed.

For an ecommerce operator: if your merchandising lead is carrying the whole category alone, give their analysts ownership of subcategories, expand their remit, and require complete work before you widen the lead's remit.
caveats: This is a single coaching case from the source, not a general rule about promotion timing.
The source's assessment tool for identifying such gaps is external; verify current availability.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Give yourself permission to out-lead a diminishing boss
cards.summary: You are not required to imitate a boss who micromanages; leading better than your manager is possible and the results make the case.
cards.use_when: You want to run your ecommerce function differently — more ownership, more debate, fewer command decisions — but your manager leads the opposite way.
steps: Recognize the obstacle the source names: 'I want to lead this way, but my boss doesn't, so I can't.' The source's response to an executive named Jim was to ask whether he could be a better leader than his boss, and what would happen if he gave himself permission to.

Run a small trial in your own area rather than asking permission for a company-wide change: Jim experimented with the new practices and received positive feedback from colleagues and employees before worrying about his boss's reaction.
Shift from telling to asking, and put the spotlight on other people's knowledge rather than your own.
Expect the boss to be neutral rather than actively resistant in many cases, and let the results speak — Jim's organization performed better and he went on to become CEO of two companies.

For ecommerce work, this might mean running your own team's buyer-to-buyer reviews as debates, posting your team's scoreboard, and asking for fixes instead of issuing them, regardless of how adjacent teams are run.
caveats: This is the source's encouragement based on a single executive's trajectory, not a guarantee that a diminishing boss will tolerate it.
In some organizations, visibly out-leading your manager carries career risk; the source acknowledges a hidden assumption that people are not expected or allowed to out-lead their bosses.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx
